But every newly arrived student tablet gets an address like 169.254.77.12 and can reach almost nothing. A colleague wants to start by replacing the patch cables. What should the technician check first?
choices: Whether Spanning Tree is blocking the redundant switch paths
The routing table on the core router, for a missing route
How much of the DHCP server's scope is currently leased
The trunk links, for missing VLAN tags
questions.why: A 169.254 (APIPA) address on new clients only, while existing clients still work, points to an exhausted DHCP scope, not to cabling or routing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell apart a switching problem, a routing problem, and DHCP address pool exhaustion from the symptoms alone, and name one limit of judging by symptoms.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by looking at the device's address. If it shows 169.254.x.x, that is APIPA, meaning DHCP failed. If only new devices fail while older ones work, the DHCP scope is probably exhausted, so I check how many leases are in use. If the address is valid but the device cannot reach neighbours on its own subnet, I suspect switching: a port in the wrong VLAN, a VLAN missing from a trunk, or a broadcast storm from a loop if everything is crawling. If local traffic works but remote destinations fail, it is routing: a wrong default gateway, a missing route, or a loop that traceroute shows as repeating hops. The limit is that symptoms overlap; a slow network could be a storm or plain congestion, so I confirm with the actual tables and leases before changing anything.
rubricPoints: Checks the IP address first and recognises 169.254.x.x as APIPA meaning DHCP failed.
Links only-new-devices-failing to an exhausted DHCP scope.
Associates same-subnet failures with VLAN, trunk, or STP issues.
Associates local-works-remote-fails with default gateway or routing table problems.
Mentions routing loops showing as repeating hops or TTL expiry.
Names a limit, such as overlapping symptoms needing confirmation.

suggested.rationale: A virtual network path tracer would let the learner follow traffic hop by hop and see exactly where a wrong VLAN, missing route, or loop stops it.

lessons.plain: A network can be working yet still feel slow or choppy. Four common culprits cause this. Congestion means more traffic is trying to cross a link than the link can carry. Latency is the delay before data arrives. Packet loss means some pieces of data never arrive at all. Wireless interference is radio noise or competing signals that garble Wi-Fi. Picture a highway. Congestion is rush-hour traffic. Latency is how long the trip takes. Packet loss is cars that never reach their exit. Interference is fog that makes drivers slow down and retry. Diagnosing performance means working out which of these four is actually happening.
lessons.guessPrompt: Video calls in an office are choppy every day around 2 p.m., when everyone is online, but they are smooth at 8 a.m. Is a damaged cable the more likely cause, or something else? Why?
lessons.teach:
Each performance problem has a definition and a measurement. Bandwidth is the maximum a link can carry, such as 1 Gbps. Throughput is what actually gets through. Congestion happens when demand exceeds bandwidth. Switch and router buffers fill, which adds delay, and then the device drops packets. You spot congestion when interface utilization sits near 100 percent and output-drop counters climb. A common cause is a bottleneck, a slower link downstream of faster ones.

Latency is one-way or round-trip delay, measured in milliseconds with ping or traceroute. Jitter is variation in latency between packets. Voice and video suffer from jitter even when average latency looks fine. Packet loss is the share of packets that never arrive. It shows up as ping timeouts or as TCP retransmissions in a protocol analyzer, a tool that captures and decodes traffic.

Wireless interference comes from other radio sources, such as microwaves, Bluetooth, or neighbouring access points. When nearby access points share or overlap a channel, a slice of the radio band, devices must take turns and collide. In 2.4 GHz only channels 1, 6, and 11 do not overlap. Signal strength is reported as RSSI, in negative dBm, where -50 is strong and -85 is weak. SNR, the signal-to-noise ratio, compares signal to background noise, and a low SNR forces slow data rates and retries.

Here is the 2 p.m. example, traced step by step. First, ping the gateway: latency jumps from 2 ms to 80 ms and loss reaches 3 percent, but only in the afternoon. Second, check the uplink: it is at 98 percent utilization with rising drops. That points to congestion, not a fault, because a bad cable would cause errors at all hours. The fix is more bandwidth or QoS, meaning quality-of-service rules that prioritize voice.

A common mistake is blaming Wi-Fi interference without first checking whether wired users suffer too. If they do, the problem sits upstream of the wireless network. Left unfixed, congestion and loss cause dropped calls, timeouts, and retransmissions that add even more load.

questions.prompt: A small law firm says Wi-Fi video calls in its conference room are choppy. A technician works through it. Step 1: Ping the gateway from a wired desktop in the same room. It shows 1 ms latency and 0 percent loss all day, so the wired network and uplink look healthy. Step 2: Check a laptop on the Wi-Fi. RSSI is -58 dBm, which is fairly strong, but SNR is low and the laptop shows many retries. Step 3: A Wi-Fi scan shows the firm's access point on 2.4 GHz channel 9. Two strong neighbouring access points sit on channels 1 and 6. Step 4: ??? Which action best completes Step 4?
choices: Replace the patch cable to the access point, because retries point to a faulty cable
Order a faster uplink from the ISP, because the retries show the internet link is congested
Move the firm's access point to channel 11, so it no longer overlaps the neighbours on 1 and 6
Move the firm's access point to channel 7, so it sits farther from the neighbour on channel 6
questions.why: Wired users are fine, so the fault is in the wireless network, and channel 11 is the only one of the non-overlapping 1, 6, and 11 that neither neighbour is using.

questions.prompt: A design studio's video calls freeze and stutter. A test shows the average round-trip time to the call server is a steady-looking 35 ms. However, packet-by-packet the delay swings between 6 ms and 140 ms. Which performance problem best describes this?
choices: Low bandwidth on the uplink
Weak signal strength, shown by RSSI
Jitter, meaning variation in latency between packets
Packet loss from a bad cable
questions.why: Jitter is variation in latency between packets, and it hurts voice and video even when the average latency looks fine.

questions.prompt: A distribution warehouse has a 10 Gbps core switch feeding a 100 Mbps link to a satellite office. During the busy morning shift, that 100 Mbps link shows 99 percent utilization and its output-drop counters keep rising. Overnight, utilization is low and there are no drops. What is the most likely cause?
choices: A damaged cable on the 100 Mbps link that corrupts frames
High jitter caused by a weak RSSI reading
Congestion at a bottleneck, where a slower link sits downstream of faster ones
Wireless interference from a microwave oven at the satellite office
questions.why: Near-100-percent utilization with climbing output drops only at busy times means demand exceeds the slow link's bandwidth, while a bad cable would cause errors at all hours.

questions.prompt: At a school, staff complain that pages load slowly over Wi-Fi. A technician immediately changes every access point's channel, but nothing improves. Later they learn that teachers on wired desktops have also been seeing ping timeouts. What did the technician get wrong?
choices: They blamed Wi-Fi interference without first checking wired users, and the problem sits upstream of the wireless network
They should have measured throughput only, since latency and loss do not affect users
They should have picked overlapping channels so access points could share airtime
They should have increased the access points' RSSI to a weaker value such as -85 dBm
questions.why: When wired users suffer too, the fault is upstream of the wireless network, so changing Wi-Fi channels cannot fix it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell congestion apart from wireless interference when users say the network is slow. Name one limit of relying on ping alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I check who is affected and when. If wired and wireless users both slow down at busy times, I suspect congestion. I would confirm it by finding a link near full utilization with climbing output drops on the switch or router, since buffers fill and then discard packets. If only Wi-Fi users suffer, I look at the radio side instead: RSSI, SNR, and whether neighbouring access points share or overlap a channel. Low SNR or a crowded channel means retries and slow data rates. Ping is useful for latency and loss, but it has limits. It shows that a delay exists, not why it exists. Some devices also deprioritize ping replies, so the numbers can mislead. And ping says little about jitter's effect on voice. Interface counters, a Wi-Fi analyzer, or a packet capture showing retransmissions fill those gaps.
rubricPoints: Defines congestion as demand exceeding bandwidth and links it to high utilization and drops.
Distinguishes latency, jitter, and packet loss and how each is measured.
Uses wired-versus-wireless comparison to locate the problem before blaming Wi-Fi.
Names wireless evidence such as channel overlap, RSSI, or low SNR.
States a limit of ping, such as showing symptoms but not causes, or deprioritized replies.

suggested.rationale: This skill is best built by reasoning through exam-style symptom scenarios and picking the right measurement, and no current mission or planned engine simulates link utilization or Wi-Fi channels.

lessons.plain: Network troubleshooting tools are the instruments a technician uses to see what a network is actually doing instead of guessing. Each one looks at a different layer of the problem. A cable tester checks the physical wire. A Wi-Fi analyzer listens to the radio airwaves. Command-line tools ask simple questions, such as whether a machine can be reached or which route traffic takes. A protocol analyzer records the actual messages crossing the wire. Think of a doctor with a stethoscope, a thermometer, an X-ray and a blood test. Each tool answers one question well, and good diagnosis means choosing the right one for the symptom.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user says one website will not load, but every other site works fine. Before learning any tools, what simple question would you want answered first, and how might you test it?
lessons.teach:
A troubleshooting tool is anything that turns an invisible network fault into evidence. Four families matter here.

Cable testers work on the physical cable. A basic tester checks continuity, meaning each wire connects end to end in the right order. A certifier also measures whether the cable meets its speed rating. A TDR (time-domain reflectometer) sends a pulse and times its echo to find how far away a break is. A toner and probe traces which wall jack connects to which switch port.

Wi-Fi analyzers listen to wireless radio. They show nearby networks, their channels, and signal strength in dBm (decibel-milliwatts, where -50 is strong and -85 is weak). That lets you spot overlapping channels or dead zones.

CLI (command-line interface) tools are typed commands. ping sends ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo requests to test reachability. traceroute (tracert on Windows) lists each hop, meaning each router, along a path. nslookup and dig query DNS, the system that turns names into IP addresses. ipconfig, ifconfig and ip show a host's own address settings. arp shows the IP-to-hardware-address table. netstat and ss list open connections and listening ports. nmap scans which ports a host exposes.

Protocol analyzers, such as Wireshark or tcpdump, capture and decode every packet, meaning each unit of data sent across the network.

Worked example: one website fails. First, ipconfig shows a valid address, so the host is configured. Next, ping to the site's IP address succeeds, so routing works. Then nslookup of the name returns no answer. The fault is DNS, and you found it without touching a cable.

A common mistake is reading a failed ping as proof that a host is down. Many firewalls block ICMP. A server can drop pings and still serve web pages. If you trust a failed ping alone, you may reboot healthy equipment while the real fault stays in place. Confirm with a second tool, such as a port check or a packet capture.

questions.prompt: At a veterinary clinic, the reception printer has stopped responding, and the wall jack behind it has no label. The technician works through the problem like this. Step 1: A toner and probe shows that the jack connects to switch port 14, and that port is active. Step 2: A basic cable tester on that run shows that one wire has no continuity, so the cable is broken somewhere. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: The technician opens the ceiling about 22 meters from the jack, finds a cable crushed by a ceiling panel, and replaces that section. Which tool belongs in Step 3?
choices: Use a TDR to send a pulse down the cable and time its echo to find how far away the break is
Use the toner and probe again to confirm the jack-to-port mapping
Use a cable certifier to check whether the cable meets its speed rating
Use a Wi-Fi analyzer to check the signal strength near the printer
questions.why: A TDR times a pulse's echo to measure the distance to a break, which is how the technician knew to look about 22 meters along the cable.

questions.prompt: A library's study room has poor Wi-Fi. A technician runs a Wi-Fi analyzer at two spots. Spot A reads -48 dBm and Spot B reads -83 dBm. What does this tell the technician?
choices: Spot B has a weak signal and may be a dead zone, while Spot A has a strong signal
Spot A has the weaker signal because its number is closer to zero
The readings show the two spots are on overlapping channels
Both readings mean the same signal strength, because dBm only shows the channel
questions.why: In dBm, a value near -50 is strong and a value near -85 is weak, so Spot B at -83 dBm is the weak area.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's staff can load the intranet web page normally. When a junior technician pings the intranet server, every request times out. What is the best next step?
choices: Declare the server down and reboot it
Run nslookup, because a failed ping always means a DNS problem
Replace the cable between the server and the switch
Confirm with a second tool, such as a port check or a packet capture, because a firewall may simply be blocking ICMP
questions.why: Many firewalls block ICMP echo requests, so a server can ignore pings and still serve pages. A failed ping alone does not prove the host is down.

questions.prompt: An administrator is logged into a bakery chain's order server and wants to list the open connections and the ports the server itself is listening on. Which tool fits this task?
choices: traceroute
dig
arp
netstat or ss
questions.why: netstat and ss list a host's open connections and listening ports. arp shows the IP-to-hardware-address table, traceroute lists the routers along a path, and dig queries DNS.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a cable tester, a Wi-Fi analyzer, a CLI tool and a protocol analyzer for a given symptom, and name one limit of at least one of these tools.
lessons.modelAnswer: I pick the tool that matches the layer where the symptom points. If the link light is off or a wired connection drops, I use a cable tester. A TDR can even tell me how far down the cable a break is. If wireless is slow or drops in certain rooms, a Wi-Fi analyzer shows signal strength and channel overlap. For most other problems, I start with CLI tools. I use ipconfig or ip for the host's own settings, ping for reachability, traceroute for where the path stops, and nslookup or dig for name resolution. When those still can't explain the fault, I use a protocol analyzer like Wireshark to see the actual packets. One limit is that ping relies on ICMP, which firewalls often block, so a failed ping doesn't prove a host is down. Another is that protocol analyzers produce a lot of data and need filtering to be useful.
rubricPoints: Matches each tool family to the layer or symptom it diagnoses.
Names specific CLI tools and what each answers, such as ping, traceroute and nslookup.
Explains that cable testers and TDRs check physical wiring and locate breaks.
Explains that Wi-Fi analyzers show channels and signal strength.
States that protocol analyzers capture and decode actual packets.
Names a real limit, such as ICMP being blocked or capture data being overwhelming.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right tool for a described symptom, so reasoning through scenario-style situations builds that skill better than any single existing mission.

scenarios.title: Splitting the Office Network at Larkspur Print Studio
scenarios.scenario:
Larkspur Print Studio is a small fictional design shop that is moving into a new office, and you are the new junior network technician. The office has three main pieces of equipment. The first is a router, a device that connects separate networks and forwards traffic between them using IP addresses. The second is a 24-port switch, a device that connects computers inside one network and forwards traffic to the right port using each computer's MAC address, which is a hardware address burned into its network card. The third is a firewall, a device that allows or blocks traffic based on rules.

The internet service provider (ISP) has given the studio one address for the router's internet-facing side: 64.40.12.10. Inside the office, the owner wants to use 192.168.10.0/24. The "/24" is a CIDR prefix, a short way of saying how many of the 32 bits in an IPv4 address identify the network. The rest of the bits identify individual devices, called hosts. The owner wants this block split into two equal subnets, which are smaller networks carved out of a larger one. One subnet is for staff computers and the other is for guest Wi-Fi.

After setup, staff report a strange problem. Typing a website's name, such as a supplier's web address, gives an error. Typing that same site's numeric IP address loads the page fine. A colleague recently added a firewall rule that blocks a list of ports. A port is a number that tells a receiving device which service or program the traffic is meant for.

1. Classify 64.40.12.10 and 192.168.10.0/24 as public or private addresses, and explain the difference in how each can be used.
2. Split 192.168.10.0/24 into two equal subnets. For each subnet, give the new prefix, the network address, the broadcast address, the usable host range, and the number of usable hosts.
3. Name the OSI layer at which the router works and the OSI layer at which the switch works, and explain why they sit at different layers. The OSI model is a seven-layer reference model describing how network communication is divided into jobs.
4. Identify which protocol is most likely being blocked, the port number it uses, and why the symptom points to it.
subParts: OSI layers of router and switch
modelAnswer: 64.40.12.10 is a public address. It falls outside the reserved private ranges, so it is unique on the internet and can be routed (forwarded) across it. 192.168.10.0/24 is a private address block. It sits inside the 192.168.0.0/16 private range. The other private ranges are 10.0.0.0/8 and 172.16.0.0/12. Private addresses can be reused freely inside any organisation, but internet routers will not forward them. So the office computers use 192.168.10.x addresses internally. When they reach the internet, the router translates their traffic to appear as coming from the public address 64.40.12.10. A common mistake is treating any address starting with 192 or 172 as private, when only the specific ranges listed above are private.

To make two equal subnets, borrow one host bit, so the prefix changes from /24 to /25. A /25 leaves 7 host bits, which gives 2 to the power of 7 = 128 addresses per subnet. Subtract 2, because the first address is the network address and the last is the broadcast address, which reaches every host in the subnet. That leaves 126 usable hosts. Subnet 1 (for example, staff) is 192.168.10.0/25. Its network address is 192.168.10.0, its broadcast is 192.168.10.127, and its usable range is 192.168.10.1 to 192.168.10.126, giving 126 hosts. Subnet 2 (for example, guests) is 192.168.10.128/25. Its network address is 192.168.10.128, its broadcast is 192.168.10.255, and its usable range is 192.168.10.129 to 192.168.10.254, giving 126 hosts. A common mistake is forgetting to subtract the network and broadcast addresses and claiming 128 usable hosts. Assigning a device one of those reserved addresses causes it to fail to communicate.

The router works at Layer 3, the Network layer. It makes forwarding decisions using IP addresses and moves traffic between different networks, such as between the staff subnet, the guest subnet, and the internet. The switch works at Layer 2, the Data Link layer. It forwards frames, the Layer 2 units of data, within a single network using MAC addresses, and it learns which MAC address is reachable on which port. They sit at different layers because they read different addresses for different jobs: the router reads IP addresses to move traffic between networks, and the switch reads MAC addresses to move traffic within one network. For that reason, the staff and guest subnets need the router (a Layer 3 device) to communicate with each other or reach the internet. A basic Layer 2 switch alone cannot move traffic between subnets.

The blocked protocol is most likely DNS (Domain Name System), which uses port 53. DNS is the service that translates a human-readable name into an IP address, much like a phone book lookup. The symptom fits exactly. Browsing by numeric IP address works, which proves that routing and HTTP/HTTPS (web traffic on ports 80 and 443) are not blocked. Browsing by name fails, which shows that only the name-to-address lookup is broken. The fix is to remove port 53 from the firewall's block list, or to allow it to the studio's DNS server. Allow both UDP and TCP on port 53: UDP handles most lookups, while TCP is used for larger responses. A common mistake is assuming the web ports are blocked and opening 80 or 443, which changes nothing. Until DNS is restored, almost every name-based service (web, email, software updates) will appear broken to users.

scenarios.title: Redundant gateway and guest Wi-Fi at Tidewater Seed Company
scenarios.scenario:
Tidewater Seed Company is a fictional 40-person business with one office and an attached warehouse. You are the new junior network technician, and your lead asks you to plan four changes. Here are the facts and terms you need.

A router is a device that forwards traffic between different networks. A default gateway is the router address that a computer sends traffic to when the destination is outside its own network. The office has one internal network, 10.20.0.0/24, and one internet connection. The internet provider gives Tidewater exactly one public IP address, an address that is reachable on the internet. Every internal device uses a private IP address, an address reserved for internal use that internet routers will not carry.

Routing can be static or dynamic. Static routing means an administrator types each route in by hand. It uses no extra bandwidth or processing, but it does not adjust by itself if a link fails. Dynamic routing means routers run a routing protocol, a set of rules they use to share and update routes automatically. It suits networks with many paths that change, but it adds complexity a single-exit network does not need. A default route is a single static route that says to send anything not otherwise known toward one next hop, here the internet provider.

NAT (Network Address Translation) is a router feature that rewrites the private source address of outgoing traffic into a public one. PAT (Port Address Translation) is a form of NAT that lets many internal devices share one public address. It tells their conversations apart by also rewriting the port number, a number that identifies one conversation on a device. One-to-one NAT needs one public address per internal device that is talking at the same time.

The office currently has one router, so if it fails, nobody reaches the internet. Your lead has bought a second router. An FHRP (First Hop Redundancy Protocol) is a protocol that lets two or more routers share a VIP (virtual IP address), a gateway address that does not belong to any single physical router. One router is active and answers for the VIP. If it stops responding, the standby router takes over the same VIP. Computers keep using that one gateway address and need no changes.

A switch connects devices within a network. A VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) is a setting on a switch that splits one physical switch into separate logical networks. Devices in different VLANs cannot talk directly; their traffic must pass through a router or firewall, a device that allows or blocks traffic based on rules. The company wants guest Wi-Fi for visiting farmers that cannot reach the staff file server.

For wireless, an SSID (Service Set Identifier) is the network name a Wi-Fi access point broadcasts. An access point can broadcast several SSIDs, and each SSID can be mapped to its own VLAN. A channel is the slice of radio frequency an access point transmits on. In the 2.4 GHz band, only channels 1, 6 and 11 do not overlap. Nearby access points on overlapping channels interfere and slow each other down. WPA3 is the current Wi-Fi security standard that encrypts wireless traffic, meaning it scrambles it so outsiders cannot read it. WPA3-Personal uses one shared passphrase. WPA3-Enterprise checks each user's own login against a central authentication server, a system that verifies who someone is. An omnidirectional antenna spreads signal in all directions around it. A directional antenna focuses signal in one direction over a longer distance. The warehouse is a long, narrow building whose access point mounts on the far end wall, and the office needs even coverage from a ceiling-mounted access point in the middle of the room. The office has three access points close together using 2.4 GHz.

Your tasks:
1. Choose static or dynamic routing for the internet connection, and choose NAT or PAT for internet access. Explain why the near-miss alternative for each is not the right fit.
2. Explain how to add the second router so the internet survives a router failure without reconfiguring every computer. Explain why giving half the computers the second router's own address as their gateway is not good enough.
3. Design the guest Wi-Fi so guests cannot reach the file server. Explain why a separate guest SSID with its own passphrase alone does not achieve this.
4. Choose channels for the three office access points, an encryption and authentication option for the staff SSID, and an antenna type for the office and for the warehouse. Justify each choice.
modelAnswer: Use static routing, in the form of a single default route pointing to the internet provider. There is only one exit, so there is nothing for a routing protocol to choose between or adapt to. Dynamic routing would add complexity and overhead with no benefit here. Use PAT on the router so all 40 or more private-addressed devices share the one public address, told apart by port numbers. One-to-one NAT would need a separate public address for each device talking at once. Tidewater has only one public address, so most devices could not reach the internet.

Configure an FHRP on both routers so they share one virtual IP (VIP). Set every computer's default gateway to the VIP. One router is active and answers for the VIP. If it fails, the standby router takes over the same VIP automatically, and computers keep working with no changes. Splitting computers between the two routers' own real addresses is not enough. If one router dies, the computers pointed at it lose internet until someone changes their gateway by hand, so half the office would still go down.

Create a separate guest VLAN on the switches and map the guest SSID to that VLAN on the access points. Staff and the file server stay on the staff VLAN. Because devices in different VLANs cannot talk directly, guest traffic must pass through the router or firewall. There, rules allow guests out to the internet but block them from the staff network and file server. A separate guest SSID with its own passphrase only controls who can join that wireless network. If that SSID drops guests onto the same network as staff, they can still reach the file server, so the VLAN separation plus filtering is what actually isolates them.

Put the three 2.4 GHz office access points on channels 1, 6 and 11, one each. These are the only non-overlapping 2.4 GHz channels, so close neighbours will not interfere with each other. Using overlapping channels would cause interference and slow Wi-Fi. For the staff SSID, use WPA3-Enterprise. It encrypts traffic and checks each person's own login against an authentication server, so a departing employee can be removed individually. WPA3-Personal's single shared passphrase would have to be changed for everyone whenever it leaks or someone leaves. Use an omnidirectional antenna on the ceiling-mounted office access point to cover the room evenly in all directions. Use a directional antenna on the warehouse end wall to push signal down the long, narrow building. An omnidirectional antenna there would waste signal sideways and behind the wall and reach less far down the length.

scenarios.title: Northfield Tile & Stone: Recovering From a Failing Core Switch
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Northfield Tile & Stone, a fictional 120-person flooring distributor with one office and a warehouse next door, as a junior network technician. The company's core switch is the central device that connects every other switch, the servers, and the link to the warehouse. It has failed three times in the past year (8,760 hours). The repairs took 2 hours, 4 hours, and 6 hours. The vendor has also announced that this switch model is end-of-support. That means the vendor no longer releases security fixes or offers help for it, even though the switch still runs.

The owner tells you two things. First, the order database can lose at most 1 hour of new orders if disaster strikes. Second, the business must be taking orders again within 4 hours of an outage. Right now the order database is backed up once a night at 11 p.m.

Your manager explains some terms you will need. MTTR (mean time to repair) is the average time it takes to fix something after it breaks. MTBF (mean time between failures) is the average time a device runs normally between one failure and the next. RPO (recovery point objective) is the most data, measured in time, that the business accepts losing. RTO (recovery time objective) is the longest the business accepts being down before service is restored. A recovery site is a second location you can move operations to. A hot site already has working equipment and nearly current data, so it can take over in minutes. A warm site has equipment and fairly recent data but needs some setup, which takes hours. A cold site is just space and power, and getting it running takes days or longer.

The warehouse staff also complain that the link between the buildings is painfully slow every afternoon. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is the method the monitoring server uses to poll devices for counters such as interface usage. It shows that link running at 95% busy from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m., but it does not show who or what is using it. Flow data is a summary record that a router or switch exports for each conversation: source and destination address, port, and how many bytes were sent. Packet capture is a full recording of every packet's contents. Separately, the log aggregation server (one central server that collects log messages from every device) shows events from the firewall and the switches out of order, with timestamps several minutes apart for the same incident. NTP (Network Time Protocol) is the service devices use to set their clocks from a shared time source.

Finally, the company has approved replacing the core switch. Change management is the formal process of describing, approving, scheduling, and recording a change so it does not surprise anyone. Decommissioning is the orderly retirement of old equipment.

1. Using the three failures over the past year, calculate the core switch's MTTR and MTBF, and say in one sentence what each number tells the owner.
2. State the RPO and RTO in hours. Say whether the current nightly backup meets the RPO and what must change. Then choose the most suitable recovery site type and explain why.
3. Name the monitoring data you would use to find out what is filling the warehouse link in the afternoon, and explain why SNMP and packet capture are not the best first choice. Then state what you would configure to fix the out-of-order logs, and why it helps.
4. List the main items your change request for the switch replacement must include. Then name the documentation you must update afterward and the steps for decommissioning the old switch.
subParts: RPO, RTO, backups, and site type
Choosing monitoring data and fixing log timestamps
modelAnswer: MTTR is total repair time divided by the number of failures: (2 + 4 + 6) / 3 = 12 / 3 = 4 hours. MTBF is total working time divided by the number of failures. Working time is the hours in the year minus downtime: 8,760 - 12 = 8,748 hours, and 8,748 / 3 = 2,916 hours. That is about 121.5 days, or roughly four months. MTTR tells the owner that each failure costs about 4 hours of outage on average. MTBF tells the owner the switch runs only about four months on average before failing again. Together, the numbers show it is unreliable and slow to fix. A full-credit answer must show both calculations and give the correct meaning of each number. Accept MTBF = 8,760 / 3 = 2,920 hours if the learner states that they ignored downtime.

The RPO is 1 hour, because at most 1 hour of orders may be lost. The RTO is 4 hours, because ordering must be running again within 4 hours. The nightly 11 p.m. backup does not meet the RPO. A failure late in the afternoon could lose almost a full day of orders. Backups or replication (copying data to a second location) must run at least every hour, or continuously. A warm site is the best fit. It already has equipment and fairly recent data, and it can be ready in hours, which fits a 4-hour RTO. A cold site takes days, so it would miss the RTO. A hot site would also work, but it costs more than a 4-hour target requires. Accept hot site only if the learner explains that it exceeds the need and costs more. The data at whichever site is chosen must be no more than 1 hour old.

Use flow data, for example NetFlow-style records exported by the router or switch on the warehouse link. Each flow record shows source and destination address, port, and byte count. So you can rank which devices and which applications are using the most bandwidth from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m. SNMP is not enough, because it only gives totals for the interface: it proves the link is busy but not who is using it. Packet capture records every packet's full contents. That is far more data than needed, it is harder to store and read for hours of traffic, and it is better kept for deep problems with a specific conversation. To fix the out-of-order logs, configure NTP on every device (firewall, switches, servers, and the log server) so they all get time from the same trusted NTP source. With matching clocks, the log aggregation server can place events from different devices in the right order, so you can trace one incident across devices.

The change request should include: a description of the change (replacing the end-of-support core switch with a new, supported model); the reason (repeated failures, an MTTR of 4 hours, and no more vendor security fixes); the systems and users affected; a risk assessment; a step-by-step implementation plan; a tested backout or rollback plan (for example, reconnecting the old switch with its saved configuration if the new one fails); a maintenance window outside business hours; the people responsible; and formal approval before any work starts. After the change, update the network diagram (new device, model, and connections), the rack layout (new position and power), the asset inventory (add the new switch with its serial number and support dates; mark the old one as retired), and IPAM, the record of which IP addresses are assigned, if the management address changed. Also save the new configuration as the baseline (the approved known-good configuration). To decommission the old switch, back up its final configuration, then erase its configuration and stored data, including passwords and keys, so no sensitive data leaves the building. Remove it from monitoring, record its retirement and disposal in the asset inventory, and dispose of it through an approved recycler, keeping the proof of disposal. Full credit needs at least a description, an approval step, a rollback plan, and a maintenance window; at least three of the documents named; and wiping the switch plus updating the inventory.

scenarios.title: Hardening the network at Harbor Lane Coffee Roasters
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Harbor Lane Coffee Roasters, a fictional company with one roasting plant and a cafe, as a junior network technician. Right now everything sits on one flat network, meaning every device can talk directly to every other device. That includes the card payment terminals at the till, three internet-connected roasting machines (IoT devices, short for Internet of Things: everyday equipment with a network connection), staff laptops, the free customer Wi-Fi, and the company's public web shop server.

This week three things happened. First, a security scan found that the web shop server runs old software with a known flaw that lets an outsider take control of it. A public attack tool that abuses this flaw is circulating online, and a criminal group has been seen targeting small online shops with it.

Second, a customer on the guest Wi-Fi reported strange behaviour. When you investigated, you found one laptop on that Wi-Fi sending out a stream of fake ARP replies. ARP, the Address Resolution Protocol, is how a device on a local network learns which hardware (MAC) address belongs to an IP address. This laptop kept claiming that its own MAC address belonged to the router's IP address, so other devices began sending their traffic through the laptop first.

Third, the owner wants to sell coffee subscriptions online to customers in the European Union, paid by card, and asks what rules apply.

Your manager asks you to handle the following.

1. Using the web shop situation, name which part is the vulnerability, which is the exploit, which is the threat, and explain what the risk is.

2. Name the attack happening on the guest Wi-Fi, and say which part of the CIA triad (confidentiality, integrity, availability) it most directly endangers and why.

3. Propose how to segment the network, meaning split it into separate zones that cannot freely reach each other. Say where the payment terminals, roasting machines, guest Wi-Fi, and public web shop server should each go, and name one control that enforces which traffic may cross between zones.

4. Name the two compliance standards that apply to the new online subscriptions, and say what each one is about.
subParts: Classify vulnerability, exploit, threat, and risk
Identify the guest Wi-Fi attack and CIA impact
Segment the network and enforce it
modelAnswer: The vulnerability is the weakness itself: the old, unpatched software on the web shop server that contains a known flaw. The exploit is the specific method or tool that takes advantage of that weakness, here the public attack tool circulating online. The threat is the person or thing that could cause harm, here the criminal group targeting small online shops. The risk is the combination of how likely it is that the threat uses the exploit against the vulnerability and how much damage would follow. In this case the risk is high: the flaw is known, the tool is easy to get, and an active group is looking for targets, so the server could be taken over and customer or card data stolen. Patching or updating the software removes the vulnerability and lowers the risk. A good answer keeps the four terms distinct and does not call the criminal group the vulnerability or the flaw the threat.

This is ARP poisoning, also called ARP spoofing. The attacker sends fake ARP replies so other devices link the router's IP address to the attacker's MAC address. Their traffic then passes through the attacker's laptop, which is an on-path, or man-in-the-middle, position. It most directly endangers confidentiality, because the attacker can read traffic that was meant only for the router and the internet, such as unencrypted logins. It can also endanger integrity, because the attacker could change traffic as it passes through. A complete answer names ARP poisoning and links it to confidentiality, with integrity as acceptable extra credit.

Put each group in its own segment, for example its own VLAN (virtual LAN, a logically separate network sharing the same switches) or subnet. The payment terminals go in an isolated payment segment that only reaches the payment processor. The roasting machines go in a separate IoT segment, because IoT devices are often poorly secured and should not be able to reach payment or staff systems. Guest Wi-Fi goes in a guest segment that has internet access only and cannot reach any internal device. This also limits the ARP poisoning seen this week to guest traffic. The public web shop server goes in a screened subnet, sometimes called a DMZ: a zone between the internet and the internal network that outsiders can reach but that cannot freely reach inside. Staff laptops stay on an internal staff segment. To enforce the zones, use firewall rules or ACLs (access control lists, ordered rules that permit or deny traffic based on things like source, destination, and port) between segments, allowing only the traffic each zone needs. NAC (network access control, which checks a device before letting it join a network) is also an acceptable extra control. Answers that simply say 'add a firewall' without putting each device group in the right zone are incomplete.

PCI DSS, the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, applies because the company takes card payments. It sets security requirements for any organisation that stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data, such as keeping the card environment separate from other systems and protecting card data. GDPR, the General Data Protection Regulation, applies because the company will handle personal data of people in the European Union. It governs how that personal data is collected, used, protected, and kept, and it gives individuals rights over their data. A strong answer may also mention data locality: rules that some data must be stored or processed within certain countries or regions, which can affect where the subscription data is hosted.

scenarios.title: Morning Login Failures at Bramblewood Logistics
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Bramblewood Logistics, a small fictional freight company, as a junior network technician. At 9:15 on a Tuesday, the help desk gets a wave of calls from the second-floor office. Staff who left their laptops connected overnight can still reach email and the internet. Staff who arrived this morning and plugged in can't reach anything, not even the shared printer.

Some background terms first. DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is a network service that automatically hands each device an IP address, the numeric address a device uses on the network. The range of addresses DHCP is allowed to give out is called the scope, or address pool. Each address is loaned for a set time called the lease time. When the lease ends, the address can go back into the pool.

Here is what you find out. The second floor has one DHCP scope running from 192.168.20.100 to 192.168.20.200. That is 101 usable addresses. The lease time is 8 days. Yesterday, a visiting training team connected about 40 extra laptops to the second-floor network for a one-day course, and those laptops have since left the building. The lights on the switch ports used by the failing laptops are on and blinking normally. A switch is the box that connects wired devices on the same local network. On one failing laptop, you run ipconfig, a command-line tool on Windows that shows a computer's IP settings. It shows the address 169.254.33.7 and no default gateway. A default gateway is the router address a device uses to reach other networks, such as the internet.

Your manager wants to see that you follow the troubleshooting methodology, which is a fixed, ordered set of steps for solving a problem, instead of guessing.

1. You are at the first step of the methodology, identifying the problem. Describe two or three specific things you would do or ask at this step, using details from this situation.
2. Explain what the 169.254.33.7 address tells you. Then explain why the normal switch-port lights let you set aside a cabling or physical fault as the likely first suspect.
3. State your theory of the most probable cause. Name how you would test it, and propose a plan of action that fixes it.
4. After the fix, describe what you must do in the final two steps of the methodology. Include one preventive measure specific to this case.
modelAnswer: The first step, identify the problem, is about gathering facts before forming any theory. Good actions here include the following. Question the users: who is affected, and since when? Here, only devices that connected this morning on the second floor are affected. Identify the symptoms: the failing devices can't reach the internet, email, or even the local printer, while devices connected overnight work. Determine whether anything changed recently: yes, about 40 visiting training laptops joined the network yesterday. Duplicate the problem if possible: plug in a test laptop on the second floor and see whether it also fails. Finally, check the scope of the problem: other floors work, so this is limited to one network segment. Doing this first matters. Jumping straight to a fix, such as rebooting the switch, can hide the real cause and waste time.

An address starting with 169.254 is an APIPA address. APIPA stands for Automatic Private IP Addressing. A Windows device gives itself an APIPA address when it asks for a DHCP address and gets no answer or no address back. A device with an APIPA address can only talk to other devices with similar self-assigned addresses. It has no default gateway, so it can't reach the printer's real address or the internet. That explains every symptom. The switch-port lights being on and blinking show that each laptop has a working physical link and is sending and receiving signals. If a cable were cut or a port were dead, the light would usually be off or show an error. Also, many separate laptops failed at once while overnight devices on the same switch kept working. That pattern points to a shared service problem, not individual bad cables. So the physical layer is not the first suspect. If a single port did show no light, a cable tester (a handheld tool that checks each wire in a cable for breaks or mis-wiring) would be the tool to use.

Theory: the DHCP address pool is exhausted. The scope has only 101 addresses. With 8-day leases, the 40 training laptops still hold their addresses even though they've left. The pool has run out, so new devices get no lease and fall back to APIPA. Devices connected overnight still work because they already hold valid leases. To test the theory, open the DHCP server's lease list, the table of addresses currently loaned out, and confirm that all or nearly all 101 addresses are in use. You should also see many leases belonging to the training laptops. Alternatively, on a working client, run ipconfig /release and then ipconfig /renew on Windows and watch it fail to get an address. Plan of action: delete the stale leases held by the departed training laptops to free addresses immediately. Then fix the root cause. Either enlarge the scope, for example widen the range if the subnet has room, or shorten the lease time, for example to 8 hours or 1 day, so addresses come back faster. Identify potential effects before acting. Changing the scope or lease time should be done carefully, and you should confirm the new range doesn't overlap any statically assigned devices such as printers. If you lack permission to change the DHCP server, escalate to whoever owns it.

The next step is to verify full system functionality. Have the affected users run ipconfig /renew or reconnect. Confirm with ipconfig that they now get a 192.168.20.x address and a default gateway. Then check that they can actually reach the printer, email, and the internet, not just that they have an address. A preventive measure specific to this case is to put visiting or guest devices on a separate guest network with its own DHCP scope and a short lease time. That way, a large group of temporary laptops can't drain the staff pool again. Another option is to set up an alert when the scope is nearly full. The final step is to document findings, actions, and outcomes. Record the symptoms (APIPA addresses on new connections), the cause (pool exhaustion from 40 long-lease guest devices), what you changed (cleared stale leases, adjusted lease time or scope), the result, and the lesson learned. Documentation helps the next technician solve a similar problem faster.
